e.t: This Hebrew word means “firstborn,” identifying the first child born in a family. It names a person in genealogical and family settings and is also used where the firstborn is involved in birth, death, or commands. The word occurs 118 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a broad and recurring use rather than a term limited to one passage. Its exact significance in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew verb means “build.” It describes the act of constructing or establishing something, whether a physical structure, a city, or another lasting work. The word appears 377 times in the Old Testament, so it is used broadly for bringing something into existence or making it firm and established. Its normal function is to express what someone builds or causes to be built. The exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being built and the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word relates to eating or to food, expressed in English with “eat” and “meat.” It can function in a sentence as an action involving eating or as a reference to food. It occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including several uses in 2 Samuel and one in Lamentations. Its precise role depends on the surrounding sentence, but its supported meaning centers on eating and food rather than a broad abstract idea.

This Hebrew noun means “garden,” referring to a cultivated or enclosed place where plants grow. In its four Old Testament occurrences, it names a garden as a real location rather than expressing an action, quality, or person. The word appears three times in Esther and once in Song of Solomon, so its meaning remains consistent across those passages. The surrounding verse determines what is happening in that garden, but the word itself identifies the place.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “beloved,” functioning as a noun or affectionate designation for someone cherished. Across its 61 Old Testament occurrences, it appears especially often in Song of Solomon, where it serves as a personal term of love. In other passages, the surrounding sentence determines how the beloved person or relationship is being identified. Its precise force therefore depends on the immediate context, while its central idea remains someone held in loving regard.

Obil is a personal name, functioning as the identifier of an individual rather than as a descriptive word or action. It is rendered “Obil” and appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 27:30. No broader ordinary meaning is established for this word beyond its use as that name. Its precise significance in the verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself serves to identify the person named Obil.

This Hebrew word refers to “counsellors”—people serving in an advisory role. It is used as a plural noun for individuals connected with giving counsel in royal or official settings. The word appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel: 3:24, 3:27, 4:36, and 6:7. Its normal sense identifies a group of counsellors rather than one individual, while the surrounding passage determines their particular activity or situation.

This Hebrew word refers to strength or power. It appears twice in the Old Testament corpus, in 2 Kings 24:15 and Psalm 73:4. Its use points to something understood in terms of might or capability, though the precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The rendering “strength” provides the clearest supported meaning for this uncommon word.

“Ham” is a personal name in the Hebrew Bible, identifying a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In this Hebrew corpus, the word occurs once, at Genesis 14:5, and its English rendering is “Ham.” Because no broader definition or surrounding verse text is available, the safest lexical explanation is simply the personal name Ham; the verse context must identify the individual’s role.

The word is the personal name “Hatach,” identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a proper name in the Hebrew text and appears four times, all in Esther 4:5–10. The name occurs in several connected verses in that passage, while the surrounding verse supplies the fuller role and meaning of the events involving him. Thus, “Hatach” identifies the person; it is not a general descriptive word.

Abiasaph is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. This Hebrew word describes something white, or something made of linen. It appears twice in the Old Testament, both times in Esther, where English renderings use “white” and “linen.” Thus, its central sense concerns a light-colored appearance or linen material, depending on how it functions in the sentence. The surrounding wording determines whether the emphasis falls on color or on the fabric itself. Its occurrences are Esther 1:6 and Esther 8:15.

Hilen is a Hebrew proper name used to identify a particular named entity rather than express an action, quality, or general idea. It is rendered “Hilen” in the available English renderings. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 6:58. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be described further, but its function is that of a name rather than an ordinary descriptive term.

This Hebrew word means “five,” the number that comes after four and before six. It is used as a numeral to identify a quantity, count people or objects, and describe an amount in Old Testament passages. The word appears 345 times in the Hebrew Bible, so its basic sense is consistent and common rather than tied to one special setting. Its exact significance in any verse comes from the people or things being counted there.

This Hebrew word refers to a place named “Iim.” It functions as a proper place-name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, once in Numbers 33:45 and once in Joshua 15:29. Since no lexical definition is given, its supported meaning is limited to identifying this place. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the location’s role in each passage.

Ikkesh is a Hebrew personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It appears three times in the Old Testament, each time as the name “Ikkesh.” The name occurs in 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles, including lists of David’s warriors and officials. Its meaning as a personal name is not otherwise defined here, so the clearest understanding is its function as an individual’s name in these genealogical and service records.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of “scattered.” It describes something spread out rather than held together in one place. Its central picture is outward movement or becoming dispersed, whether referring to people, objects, or something that expands. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs five times in four verses. The precise force depends on the sentence, but the word consistently points toward separation, spreading, or being distributed across an area.

This Hebrew verb means “deliver.” It expresses the action of bringing a person or people out from danger, oppression, or an adverse situation. In its Old Testament uses, the word commonly describes God’s action toward those who need help, though it can also describe deliverance involving human rulers or communities. It occurs 25 times in the Hebrew Bible, with many occurrences in the Psalms.

Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

The word occurs 42 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages connected with kings, trade, speech, and giving. It is also associated with Tyre’s place among the nations and peoples mentioned in Scripture. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “parched,” describing grain or food prepared by roasting or drying. It occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, referring to food presented or carried for people to eat. Its use in passages from Leviticus, Ruth, 1 Samuel, and 2 Samuel shows a consistent connection with prepared grain rather than a person or action. The word functions as the food item or its quality, while the surrounding sentence identifies how it is used.

e.t: “Kiriathaim” is a geographical place name, used to identify a specific location rather than to describe an action, quality, or person. It functions as a proper name in the Hebrew Old Testament and appears eight times across seven verses. The same name is rendered consistently as “Kiriathaim,” with a spelling variation in some translations. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “far,” describing something at a distance or remote from a person, place, or point of reference. It can function in ordinary statements about location and distance, and its repeated use across the Old Testament shows a stable sense of remoteness. The word occurs 84 times in the Hebrew Bible, including passages from Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the Psalms. The surrounding verse determines precisely what is distant, but the central idea remains being far away.

This Hebrew word describes something “thin,” indicating a lack of thickness or fullness. It is used in the Old Testament three times, all within Genesis 41, where it functions as a descriptive word for the condition of something. Its meaning remains focused and concrete: the subject is thin rather than substantial or full-bodied. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described, but the word itself supplies this basic description.

“Temples” refers to the areas at the sides of the head, and this Hebrew noun names that bodily feature. In its five Old Testament occurrences, it is rendered “temples,” including passages in Judges and Song of Songs. The word therefore identifies a physical part of a person rather than an action or abstract quality. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “rest,” referring to what remains after others have been distinguished or considered. In a sentence, it identifies the remaining people or portion rather than the whole previously mentioned group. It occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Ezra and Daniel, where it can refer broadly to a remainder. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word describes someone or something as “bowed.” It presents a lowered or bent posture rather than an upright one, and it can function as the action or condition being expressed in a sentence. The word occurs 21 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with uses spread especially across Isaiah and Psalms. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a “request,” naming what someone asks for or seeks. It functions as a noun rather than describing an action. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Psalm 21:2. Its normal sense is therefore focused and specific: the matter presented as a request. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being requested, but the word itself identifies that requested matter.

This Hebrew noun refers to “bushes,” designating a kind of vegetation. It appears four times in the Old Testament corpus, twice in Genesis and twice in Job. Because it is a noun, it identifies the vegetation being spoken about rather than describing an action, quality, or person. Its precise reference in each passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary lexical sense is the plant growth called bushes.

This Hebrew word means “tranquillity.” It functions as a term naming a settled condition, rather than an action or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 4:27. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context, while its basic lexical sense remains tranquillity.

This Hebrew word refers to a governor or ruler—someone who possesses power and authority. It can describe a person who governs others, as well as the power or strength associated with ruling. The word appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament: once in Genesis and three times in Ecclesiastes. Its central idea is authority exercised over others, whether viewed through the ruler himself or through the power that enables him to rule.

Shamhuth is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 27:8, and English Bible renderings preserve it as “Shamhuth.” Because the available information identifies this word as a name and does not include the surrounding verse text, its precise role in that passage depends on the context there.

This word means “year”. It refers to a span of time measured as a yearly period. In the Old Testament, it appears seven times, especially in Ezra and Daniel, where it marks dates, periods of rule, or the passing of time. The plural sense refers to more than one year. Its use is straightforward and time-related, helping readers understand when something happened or how long a period lasted.

This Hebrew word refers to “enemies”—people who stand against or threaten someone. It identifies opposing people rather than an action or quality. In its five Old Testament occurrences, all in Psalms, it consistently describes those who oppose the person praying. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains people acting in hostility toward another.

Sheth is a proper name, identifying a named referent rather than describing a general idea or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears only once, in Numbers 24:17, and is rendered “Sheth.” The word therefore functions as a name within that sentence, not as a common noun with a broad definition. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person or group being named there.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “straw,” the dry plant material used with clay or mud in making bricks. It can be something provided, gathered, or withheld, and Scripture also mentions it as material given to animals. The word occurs 17 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in passages concerning brickmaking and daily provision. Its normal meaning remains concrete: straw as useful agricultural material, whether available for work or needed for ordinary care.

This Hebrew word expresses the action of “contend”—to engage in a struggle or dispute. It functions as a predicate, describing what someone does rather than naming a person or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Jeremiah: 12:5 and 22:15. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is an active act of contending.

This Hebrew verb means “plunder”: to take goods or possessions from a defeated place or people. It describes the act of seizing what remains after victory, especially in accounts of warfare and conquest. The word occurs 43 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a repeated scriptural use for taking spoil from those overcome. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.
